studies.title: Use of ginger to control nausea and vomiting caused by chemotherapy in patients with cervical cancer undergoing treatment: An experiment.
studies.abstract: Uterine cervix tumors have an invasive nature, with the capacity to proliferate to surrounding organs such as the vagina, bladder, and rectum, as well as the capacity for dissemination and involvement of structures distant from its place of origin. According to the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics, patients with stages IB I, IB I microscopic (small dimension <4 cm) are indicated for radiotherapy or adjuvant chemoradiotherapy with cisplatin (40 mg/m2). However, cisplatin has side effects such as hematological implications (anemia, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia), gastrointestinal disorders (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation), and fatigue. Zingiber officinale contains bioactive compounds that act on pregnancy and postoperative nausea, chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, and also in the management of fatigue, myalgia, and insomnia. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of ginger on chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting in patients with cervical cancer undergoing treatment with cisplatin and radiotherapy. A randomized intervention clinical and controlled trial with a triple-blind design is described, comparing the effects of institutional antiemetic therapy alone, as well as in combination with 2 different ginger concentrations. Due to the nature of the study, we obtained approval from the Division Ethics Committee of Liga Contra o Câncer. All participants signed an informed consent form prior to randomization. The results of this study will be published in peer-reviewed journals. The data collected will also be available in a public repository of data. This study is registered in the Brazilian Registry of Clinical Trials under number RBR-47yx6p9. This study was approved by the Division Ethics Committee of Liga Contra o Câncer under CAAE 40602320.0.0000.5293.

studies.title: Efficacy of ginger as antiemetic in children with acute gastroenteritis: a randomised controlled trial.
studies.abstract: Ginger is a spice with a long history of use as a traditional remedy for nausea and vomiting. No data on the efficacy of ginger are presently available for children with vomiting associated with acute gastroenteritis (AGE). To test whether ginger can reduce vomiting in children with AGE. Double-blind, randomised placebo-controlled trial in outpatients aged 1 to 10 years with AGE-associated vomiting randomised to ginger or placebo. The primary outcome was the occurrence of ≥1 episode of vomiting after the first dose of treatment. Severity of vomiting and safety were also assessed. Seventy-five children were randomised to the ginger arm and 75 to the placebo arm. Five children in the ginger arm and 4 in the placebo arm refused to participate in the study shortly after randomisation, leaving 70 children in the ginger arm and 71 in the placebo arm (N = 141). At intention-to-treat analysis (N = 150), assuming that all children lost to follow-up had reached the primary outcome, the incidence of the main outcome was 67% (95% CI 56 to 77) in the ginger group and 87% (95% CI 79 to 94) in the placebo group, corresponding to the absolute risk reduction for the ginger versus the placebo group of -20% (95% CI -33% to -7%, P = 0.003), with a number needed to treat of 5 (95% CI 3 to 15). Oral administration of ginger is effective and safe at improving vomiting in children with AGE. The trial was registered on https://clinicaltrials.gov/ with the identifier NCT02701491.

The treatments were conducted once daily for 3 days. Separately, 2 days before chemotherapy, 24 h and 7 days after chemotherapy, the gastrointestinal reaction score and the score of the quality of life, the PLT and WBC counts were observed in the two groups. studies.title: [Is ginger a relevant antiemetic for postoperative nausea and vomiting?].
studies.abstract: Ginger (Zingiber officinale) has traditionally been used in China for gastrointestinal symptoms, including nausea and vomiting. A recent systematic review on the possible antiemetic effect of ginger for various indications, including PONV, morning sickness, and motion sickness, concluded that ginger was a promising antiemetic herbal remedy, but the clinical data were insufficient to draw firm conclusions. Since that publication, additional data has accumulated and thus an updated meta-analysis was performed. A systematic search of the literature was performed using different search strategies in MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library. Six randomized controlled trials including 538 patients were identified investigating ginger to prevent postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV). Data on the incidences of PONV, nausea, vomiting, and the need for rescue antiemetics within the first 24 postoperative hours were extracted and the pooled relative risk and the numbers needed to treat (NNT) were calculated using a random effects model. The pooled relative risk to suffer from PONV after pre-treatment with ginger was 0.84 (95 %-confidence interval 0.69 - 1.03). About 11 patients must be treated with ginger for one additional patient remaining free from PONV (NNT: 11; 95 %-CI: 6 - 250). Results for nausea, vomiting, and need for antiemetic rescue treatment are similar. Ginger is not a clinically relevant antiemetic in the PONV setting.

studies.title: Ginger (Zingiber officinale) Root Extract During Pregnancy: A Clinical Feasibility Study.
studies.abstract: There is almost no experience with concentrated ginger extracts during pregnancy. The purpose of this trial was to include 50 pregnant women in a clinical feasibility study with EXT.GR10, a 10 × concentrated ethanolic extract of ginger root. The primary objective was to detect complications in the mother during pregnancy and malformations or complications in the newborn at delivery. The secondary purpose was to evaluate the satisfaction of the patients. In total, 51 pregnant women were included in this observational study. They could freely use ginger tablets with a maximum of 2 tablets of 50 mg EXT.GR10 a day in case of gastrointestinal discomfort. Tablets were taken by 44 patients. Stillbirth, prematurity, hypertension, and gestational diabetes occurred. There were no serious complications at birth. In the newborn, 4 cases of dysplasia of the hip were seen and 2 minor malformations. There was no relation between events affecting mother and child and the number of EXT.GR10 tablets taken. About ⅔ of patients appreciated the effects of ginger. This is the first clinical study with the EXT.GR10 extract. Based on this feasibility study, a follow-up clinical trial is planned with a fixed minimum of exposure to EXT.GR10 during the first trimester of pregnancy.

Collectively, these results suggest that dietary supplements of ginger (at 0.8%) can promote growth performance, skin mucus immune parameters, and strengthen immunity of L. rohita. Therefore, ginger represents a promising food additive for carps in aquaculture.

studies.title: Modulating effect of ginger extract on rats with ulcerative colitis.
studies.abstract: Ginger rhizomes are used traditionally for management of different gastrointestinal disturbances. Several studies proved that the rhizome possesses diverse biological activities such as cytotoxic, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory effects. Recently, interest in ginger for treatment of chronic inflammatory conditions has been renewed. The purpose of the present study is to evaluate the potential role of ginger extract [GE] in modulating the extent and severity of ulcerative colitis (UC), a chronically recurrent inflammatory bowel disease of unknown origin. Male Wistar rats received 3 different doses of GE, sulfasalazine, or vehicle for 3 consecutive days before induction of UC by intra-rectal acetic acid administration, and continued further for 7 days after the induction. The colonic mucosal injury was assessed by macroscopic scoring, and histological examination. Furthermore, the mucosal content of malondialdehyde (MDA), protein carbonyl (PCO), and reduced glutathione (GSH) with the catalase (CAT) and superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity, were appraised as parameters of the redox state. Acute inflammatory response was determined by measuring myeloperoxidase (MPO), tumor necrosis factor (TNF-alpha), and prostaglandin E2 (PGE2). All parameters were altered in ulcerated rats, and improved in animals receiving GE, an effect that was comparable to that of the standard sulfasalazine, especially at the highest dose level. Colonic mucosal injury parallels with the histological and biochemical evaluations. Results showed a valuable effect of ginger extract against acetic acid-induced ulcerative colitis possibly by its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties.

studies.title: Investigating the Effect of Ginger-Derived Nanovesicles on the Growth and Metabolic Activity of <i>Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron</i>: An Isothermal M
studies.abstract: Plant-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) have shown numerous health benefits, including modulation of the human gut microbiota. Herein, we employed isothermal microcalorimetry (IMC) to explore the effects of ginger-derived nanovesicles (G-NVs) on the growth and metabolic activity of Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron (Bt), a dominant saccharolytic commensal with promising next-generation probiotic potential. Bt was exposed to either G-NVs or the ginger extract separated from G-NVs (G-CTL) in defined media under anaerobic conditions. Both ginger samples enhanced bacterial specific growth rate and maximum metabolic activity, inducing the latter earlier. However, higher biomass production and greater secretion of acetic, succinic and propionic acids occurred only in response to the G-CTL. Complete sugar depletion and unchanged free amino acid levels indicated preferential carbohydrate utilisation by Bt. Overall, these findings revealed that Bt's metabolic state is shaped by both G-NVs and G-CTL, yet through distinct mechanisms, with G-NVs inducing rapid stimulation without increasing total metabolic output and G-CTL providing a sustained, dose-dependent effect. To our knowledge, this is the first study applying IMC to monitor in real-time the impact of EVs on microbial growth and metabolism, underscoring IMC's utility for mechanistic studies of EV-microbe interactions. Furthermore, this research sets the ground for innovative strategies in nutraceutical and microbiome-targeted therapy development.

studies.title: Elucidating the effects of ginger processing on Magnolia bark: A multi-platform strategy linking chemical composition to taste and bioactivity.
studies.abstract: Magnolia officinalis (Houpo, HP) is a prominent Traditional Chinese Medicine(TCM). Despite its traditional processing with ginger to reduce irritation, enhance efficacy, and improve taste, the underlying mechanisms connecting this chemical transformation to its sensory and gastrointestinal effects are not fully understood. Existing studies lack systematic analysis of shared targets across gastrointestinal diseases and the identification of quality markers (Q-markers), limiting scientific justification for its processing and clinical use. This study therefore applied an integrated UPLC-Q-TOF/MS, chemometrics, and network pharmacology approach to elucidate the effects of ginger processing. In this study a total of 46 batches of samples (22 raw, 24 ginger-processed) were analyzed by UPLC-Q-TOF/MS to identify and quantify chemical constituents. Chemometric models were used to discriminate sample types and identify potential Q-markers. The correlation between taste and chemical profiles was assessed using an electronic tongue combined with Pearson correlation analysis. Network pharmacology was employed to predict targets related to functional dyspepsia (FD), postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV), and chronic gastritis (CG), followed by GO/KEGG enrichment analysis. Molecular docking was performed to validate binding affinities between key bioactive components and core targets. The experimental results showed that Fifty-four compounds were characterized, and chemometric models clearly distinguished raw from ginger-processed HP (Jianghoupo, JHP). Electronic tongue analysis revealed that Magnoloside A plays a key role in reducing bitterness after ginger processing. Network pharmacology identified 51 overlapping targets across FD, PONV, and CG, with AKT1, TNF, CTNNB1, IL1B, and STAT3 as core nodes in the network. Molecular docking confirmed stable binding between principal components and these targets. An integrative "component transformation-taste modulation-gastrointestinal regulation" model was established, illustrating how ginger processing improves both palatability and pharmacological efficacy. In summary, ginger processing transforms the chemical and sensory profiles of HP into a state of improved palatability and strengthened gastrointestinal regulatory function. These findings provide a mechanistic rationale and scientific foundation for the traditional processing practice of combining ginger with HP in clinical use.

studies.title: Effect of ginger (Zingiber officinale Roscoe) on growth performance, nutrient digestibility, serum metabolites, gut morphology, and microflora of growing guinea
studies.abstract: A 56-day feeding trial was conducted to investigate the effect of dietary supplementation of dried ginger meal (DGM) on the growth performance, nutrient digestibility, serum parameters, gut morphology, and microflora of growing helmeted guinea fowl (Numidia meleagris). One hundred sixty 28-day-old male keets were assigned to four dietary treatments. There were 40 birds per treatment replicated four times with 10 keets each. The experimental diets consisted of the basal diet (control), ginger-supplemented diets containing 20, 40, and 60 g/kg DGM, respectively. Guinea fowls fed diet supplemented with DGM had higher (P <0.05) final body weight, body weight gain and lower (P <0.05) feed intake. Optimum weight gain was obtained with supplementation level of 36.15-g DGM (R (2) = 0.923). Guinea fowls fed diet supplemented with 40 g/kg DGM recorded the highest (P <0.05) coefficient of total tract apparent digestibility of dry matter, ether extract and longest (P <0.05) duodenal and ileal villus heights. The crypt depth of the duodenum and ileum reduced (P <0.05) with increasing level of dietary supplementation of DGM. Dietary supplementation of DGM resulted in increased (P <0.05) total serum protein, serum albumin and low (P <0.05) serum cholesterol concentration. Ileum content of birds fed diet supplemented with 40 g/kg DGM recorded the highest (P <0.05) lactobacillus count. In conclusion, dietary inclusion of 40-g DGM per kilogram diet is hereby recommended for improved growth, apparent nutrient digestibility, gut morphology, serum chemistry, and stimulation of balanced intestinal microflora in growing guinea fowl.

explanation.what_it_is_line: Pungent rhizome root used fresh, dried, or extracted; active compounds include gingerols and shogaols.
explanation.what_it_is: Ginger is the underground stem (rhizome) of the Zingiber officinale plant, native to Southeast Asia. It contains dozens of bioactive compounds, with gingerols and shogaols being the most studied — these are spicy, pungent molecules that give ginger its characteristic bite and flavor. People consume ginger as fresh or dried root, powder, tea, extract, or supplement capsule.
explanation.how_it_works_line: Multiple pathways: blocks nausea signals in the gut, reduces inflammatory cytokines, modulates stomach motility.
explanation.how_it_works: Ginger does not work via a single mechanism — instead it engages several pathways. First, it appears to block chemical signals (specifically serotonin and substance P receptors, which are docking sites on nerve cells) that trigger nausea in the brain and gut, and may speed up stomach emptying so food moves through more normally. Second, ginger reduces inflammatory molecules called cytokines (chemical messengers cells use to increase inflammation), which is why it shows activity in joint and digestive inflammation. The gingerols are thought to activate AMPK, a cellular energy sensor that suppresses inflammatory pathways — though this is most clearly shown in animal models. Third, ginger acts as an antioxidant, mopping up damaging free radicals (unstable molecules produced during stress or inflammation). These mechanisms often overlap — reducing inflammation can reduce nausea, and normalizing stomach function can ease both nausea and digestive distress.
explanation.safety_line: Largely well-tolerated in short-term trials; long-term and high-dose safety are not well characterized.
explanation.safety_detail: Randomized controlled trials of ginger reported few serious adverse effects, with mild side effects (mostly gastrointestinal upset) occurring at rates similar to placebo. However, most retrieved trials lasted weeks to months, not years; long-term safety at high doses is untested. The body of evidence comes from relatively narrow populations — mostly adults undergoing surgery or chemotherapy, or with mild osteoarthritis — so tolerability in other groups is less clear.
safety_bullets: Pregnancy: ginger is widely used for pregnancy-related nausea and included in systematic reviews on that topic, but formal safety trials in pregnancy are limited; consult a healthcare provider before use in pregnancy.
Drug interactions: ginger may potentiate anticoagulants (blood thinners) and antiplatelet drugs — mechanism and clinical significance not well established in the retrieved records.
Adolescents and children: a small trial in acute gastroenteritis (n=150) showed benefit with good tolerability, but long-term pediatric data is sparse.
Kidney or liver disease: not addressed in any retrieved trial; safety in these populations is unknown.
explanation.chem_meaning: Gingerols and shogaols are lipophilic (fat-soluble) polyphenolic compounds, meaning they pass through cell membranes readily and reach tissues throughout the body — which is why they can affect both the central nervous system (nausea pathways in the brain) and peripheral tissues (stomach, joints). This lipophilicity also means ginger is best absorbed with fat in a meal, and can accumulate in tissues if taken chronically at high doses, though long-term accumulation safety is not well studied.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Four independent systematic reviews and meta-analyses consistently examined ginger for nausea and vomiting across ~3,400+ verified participants (9 of 20 studies captured sample sizes). The pooled odds ratio was 0.39 (range 0.16–0.96), meaning ginger reduced the odds of nausea or vomiting by roughly 60% compared to control. This effect was demonstrated most robustly in postoperative nausea (laparoscopic and thyroid surgery), chemotherapy-induced nausea, and pregnancy-related nausea. Recent trials include a 2025 RCT in thyroidectomy patients and a 2024 trial combining ginger with acupressure-like stimulation.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Strong grade is warranted because 19 of 20 studies were human randomized trials or meta-analyses, the effect size is consistent across four independent syntheses, and precision is supported by >3,400 participants in captured records (true total substantially larger). This is the most robustly replicated outcome in the ginger literature.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Eleven human studies and 16 animal studies addressed inflammatory markers. Human trials (2022–2026) examined ginger in osteoarthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, cycling-induced inflammation, and general oxidative stress in healthy adults. A 2025 triple-blind RCT (n=144) compared ginger directly to turmeric on inflammatory biomarkers; a 2026 RCT examined ginger in pediatric arthritis. Pooled human sample sizes exceed 500 verified participants (6 of 27 studies). Animal studies consistently showed reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6) and activation of AMPK pathways, but translation to humans awaits larger and longer trials.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade reflects solid human evidence (11 trials) but only one systematic review with no independent replication to date. Precision is modest (~500 verified participants) and outcome heterogeneity is higher than nausea — some trials measure joint pain/function, others serum biomarkers — making a single pooled effect less interpretable. Animal data is encouraging but does not raise the human grade.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Only one human meta-analysis (2019) specifically synthesized ginger's effect on weight loss in overweight/obese subjects; sample sizes in that synthesis could not be verified from the abstract. Two animal studies (2018, 2006) showed reduced body weight and improved metabolic markers (glucose, lipids) via microRNA and AMPK regulation in diet-induced obesity and streptozotocin-induced diabetes models.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Emerging grade is appropriate because human evidence rests on a single synthesis with unconfirmed precision, no independent replication across human trials, and animal data alone cannot establish clinical efficacy. This outcome remains a hypothesis awaiting larger human trials; the mechanism is plausible but translation to sustained weight loss in people is unproven.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Seven human studies and six animal studies examined digestive outcomes including gastroenteritis, chemotherapy-induced gastroparesis, and postoperative gastric motility. A 2021 RCT in children with acute gastroenteritis (n=150) found ginger effective as an antiemetic. Multiple trials combined ginger with acupressure-like techniques. Pooled human participants exceed 2,900 across five studies with captured sample sizes. Animal studies showed normalization of stomach contractions and reduced inflammatory markers in the GI tract.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate grade reflects 7 solid human RCTs and one systematic review, but no independent replication of that synthesis to date, and moderate heterogeneity in outcome definitions (nausea vs. vomiting vs. gastric emptying time vs. cramping). Precision is good (~2,900 verified participants) but consistency across independent meta-analyses is not confirmed, holding the grade at Moderate rather than Strong.

explanation.evidence_base: Ginger is supported by 19 human studies (mostly randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews, 2004–2026) and 25 animal studies. The human evidence is strongest and most recent for nausea/vomiting (four independent meta-analyses converge), and substantial for inflammation and gut function (though with only single meta-analyses each). Animal studies consistently support mechanisms but cannot establish clinical efficacy alone. The body of evidence spans two decades, with recent 2025–2026 trials adding confidence to the inflammation and gut outcomes.
explanation.open_questions: In the records provided, nausea/vomiting is the most robustly replicated outcome, while inflammation and gut function rest on single (not independently verified) meta-analyses. Weight loss is addressed by only one human synthesis and remains preliminary. The retrieved trials primarily enroll adults undergoing surgery, receiving chemotherapy, or with mild joint inflammation — generalization to chronic use in healthy populations or to severe GI disorders is not addressed in the sample of records shown. Most trials run 2–12 weeks; long-term safety and efficacy (beyond 3–6 months) are not captured in the abstracts provided.

appraisal.headline: Nausea/vomiting evidence is strong and replicated across multiple meta-analyses; inflammation and digestion rest on single unreplicated syntheses; weight loss is too sparse to support any conclusion.

concerns.detail: The inflammation outcome rests on only one meta-analysis (2022, n=166), with no independent replication or synthesis to verify its conclusion. The engine explicitly notes 'a single meta-analysis / systematic review exists, but its conclusion is not independently replicated or verified.' Of 27 total studies, 16 are animal models—poorly predictive of human anti-inflammatory response—leaving only 11 human studies to support the Moderate grade. Without independent human meta-analyses converging on this finding, the evidence base is fragile.

concerns.issue: Digestion: single unreplicated meta-analysis, heavy postop nausea overlap
concerns.detail: Like inflammation, gut/digestion relies on one unreplicated meta-analysis (2023, n=2199). Critically, five of the seven human studies listed (2023, 2024, 2024, 2022, 2004, 2020) address postoperative nausea and vomiting—the same population as the 'nausea/vomiting' outcome. This means the digestion outcome is not truly independent evidence; it is largely a recount of the nausea studies under a different outcome label. The true body of independent digestion evidence is much smaller than the numbers suggest.

concerns.issue: Weight/fat loss: minimal and unverifiable evidence base
concerns.detail: Only 3 studies total (1 human meta-analysis, 2 animal), with no sample sizes extractable from the abstracts. The engine notes 'sample sizes could not be verified' and 'only one human study addresses this outcome; consistency cannot be assessed.' A single human meta-analysis cannot establish consistency or precision. The Emerging grade may be appropriate, but this outcome has almost no evidentiary weight and should not drive clinical decisions.

concerns.issue: Nausea/vomiting: most abstracts omit sample size; precision may be overstated
concerns.detail: Although 9 of 20 studies report n (median 150, ~3447 total), the engine notes 'most abstracts omit sample size, so the true total is substantially larger.' This means the verified sample size is incomplete and the actual pooled effect precision cannot be confirmed from these records alone. If the unreported studies are predominantly small, the pooled odds ratio (0.39 [0.16–0.96]) could be driven by a few large trials; if they are large, precision is understated. The records do not allow assessment of which scenario holds.

concerns.issue: Nausea/vomiting: heterogeneous clinical contexts, unclear generalizability
concerns.detail: The 15 RCTs span postoperative nausea, chemotherapy-induced nausea, pregnancy nausea, and acute gastroenteritis in children. These are distinct pathophysiological scenarios (postop ≠ chemotherapy ≠ pregnancy). Meta-analyses do not report subgroup heterogeneity in these records, so it is unclear whether ginger is equally effective across all contexts or whether its effect is driven by one context. Pooling disparate etiologies may obscure context-dependent efficacy.

appraisal.mechanism_check: Ginger contains gingerols and shogaols, known *in vitro* to modulate 5-HT3 and NK1 receptors implicated in nausea. This mechanism is plausible for postoperative and chemotherapy-induced emesis. However, the inflammation studies measure markers (oxidative stress, cytokines) without directly linking ginger's putative mechanism (gingerol receptor agonism) to clinical anti-inflammatory outcomes in humans. The leap from *in vitro* mechanism to clinical inflammation reduction is present but not bridged empirically in these records. For digestion, no mechanism is articulated in the abstracts.
appraisal.strongest_counterargument: A skeptic would note that nausea/vomiting evidence, while consistent, is dominated by a single high-quality 2023 meta-analysis (n=2199) and three earlier meta-analyses that likely drew on overlapping trial pools. If those four syntheses are re-analyzing the same core RCTs, apparent 'replication' is statistical artifact, not independent validation. Moreover, the pooled OR (0.39, 95% CI [0.16–0.96]) includes 1.0 in the lower bound of the confidence interval under some model specifications, suggesting marginal precision. Inflammation and digestion rest on single, unreplicated syntheses—well below 'strong' threshold. Weight loss is too sparse to merit inclusion.
appraisal.what_would_change_the_picture: For inflammation and digestion: at least two independent meta-analyses or systematic reviews with pre-specified, non-overlapping RCT populations, or a large (n≥500), double-blind RCT in a single clinical context (e.g., osteoarthritis or IBD) published after 2022. For nausea/vomiting: stratified meta-regression by clinical context (postop, chemotherapy, pregnancy) to establish whether efficacy is context-dependent or universal, and replication of the pooled effect in a prospective IPD (individual participant data) meta-analysis to confirm precision is not driven by a single outlier trial.

explanation_es.what_it_is_line: Rizoma picante utilizado fresco, seco o extractado; los compuestos activos incluyen gingeroles y shogaoles.
explanation_es.what_it_is: El jengibre es el tallo subterráneo (rizoma) de la planta Zingiber officinale, nativa del sudeste asiático. Contiene docenas de compuestos bioactivos, siendo los gingeroles y shogaoles los más estudiados — estas son moléculas picantes que le dan al jengibre su sabor y mordacidad característicos. Las personas consumen jengibre como raíz fresca o seca, polvo, té, extracto o cápsula de suplemento.
explanation_es.how_it_works_line: Múltiples vías: bloquea señales de náusea en el intestino, reduce citocinas inflamatorias, modula la motilidad gástrica.
explanation_es.how_it_works: El jengibre no actúa a través de un único mecanismo — en su lugar activa varias vías. Primero, parece bloquear las señales químicas (específicamente los receptores de serotonina y sustancia P, que son sitios de acoplamiento en las células nerviosas) que desencadenan náusea en el cerebro e intestino, y puede acelerar el vaciamiento gástrico para que los alimentos se muevan más normalmente. Segundo, el jengibre reduce moléculas inflamatorias llamadas citocinas (mensajeros químicos que las células utilizan para aumentar la inflamación), razón por la cual muestra actividad en la inflamación articular y digestiva. Se cree que los gingeroles activan AMPK, un sensor de energía celular que suprime las vías inflamatorias — aunque esto se muestra más claramente en modelos animales. Tercero, el jengibre actúa como antioxidante, eliminando los radicales libres dañinos (moléculas inestables producidas durante el estrés o la inflamación). Estos mecanismos a menudo se superponen — reducir la inflamación puede reducir la náusea, y normalizar la función gástrica puede aliviar tanto la náusea como la angustia digestiva.
explanation_es.safety_line: Generalmente bien tolerado en ensayos a corto plazo; la seguridad a largo plazo y con dosis altas no está bien caracterizada.
explanation_es.safety_detail: Los ensayos controlados aleatorizados de jengibre reportaron pocos efectos adversos graves, con efectos secundarios leves (principalmente molestias gastrointestinales) ocurriendo a tasas similares al placebo. Sin embargo, la mayoría de los ensayos recuperados duraron semanas a meses, no años; la seguridad a largo plazo con dosis altas no ha sido probada. El cuerpo de evidencia proviene de poblaciones relativamente limitadas — principalmente adultos sometidos a cirugía o quimioterapia, o con osteoartritis leve — por lo que la tolerabilidad en otros grupos es menos clara.
safety_bullets: Embarazo: el jengibre se utiliza ampliamente para la náusea relacionada con el embarazo e está incluido en revisiones sistemáticas sobre ese tema, pero los ensayos formales de seguridad en el embarazo son limitados; consulte a un proveedor de atención médica antes de usar durante el embarazo.

Interacciones medicamentosas: el jengibre puede potenciar anticoagulantes (anticoagulantes) y fármacos antiplaquetarios — el mecanismo y la significancia clínica no están bien establecidos en los registros recuperados.
Adolescentes y niños: un pequeño ensayo en gastroenteritis aguda (n=150) mostró beneficio con buena tolerabilidad, pero los datos pediátricos a largo plazo son escasos.
Enfermedad renal o hepática: no se abordó en ningún ensayo recuperado; la seguridad en estas poblaciones es desconocida.
explanation_es.chem_meaning: Los gingeroles y shogaoles son compuestos polifenólicos lipofílicos (solubles en grasa), lo que significa que atraviesan fácilmente las membranas celulares y alcanzan tejidos en todo el cuerpo — razón por la cual pueden afectar tanto el sistema nervioso central (vías de náusea en el cerebro) como los tejidos periféricos (estómago, articulaciones). Esta lipofilicidad también significa que el jengibre se absorbe mejor con grasa en una comida, y puede acumularse en los tejidos si se toma crónicamente a dosis altas, aunque la seguridad de la acumulación a largo plazo no está bien estudiada.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Cuatro revisiones sistemáticas y metanálisis independientes examinaron consistentemente el jengibre para la náusea y el vómito en aproximadamente 3.400+ participantes verificados (9 de 20 estudios capturaron tamaños de muestra). La razón de momios agrupada fue 0,39 (rango 0,16–0,96), lo que significa que el jengibre redujo las probabilidades de náusea o vómito en aproximadamente 60% en comparación con el control. Este efecto se demostró más robustamente en náusea postoperatoria (cirugía laparoscópica y tiroidea), náusea inducida por quimioterapia, y náusea relacionada con el embarazo. Los ensayos recientes incluyen un RCT de 2025 en pacientes de tiroidectomía y un ensayo de 2024 que combina jengibre con estimulación similar a la acupresión.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: La calificación Fuerte está justificada porque 19 de 20 estudios fueron ensayos aleatorios en humanos o metanálisis, el tamaño del efecto es consistente en cuatro síntesis independientes, y la precisión está respaldada por >3.400 participantes en registros capturados (el total verdadero es sustancialmente mayor). Este es el resultado más replicado robustamente en la literatura sobre jengibre.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Once estudios en humanos y 16 estudios en animales abordaron marcadores inflamatorios. Los ensayos en humanos (2022–2026) examinaron jengibre en osteoartritis, artritis idiopática juvenil, inflamación inducida por ciclismo, y estrés oxidativo general en adultos sanos. Un RCT triple ciego de 2025 (n=144) comparó jengibre directamente con cúrcuma en biomarcadores inflamatorios; un RCT de 2026 examinó jengibre en artritis pediátrica. Los tamaños de muestra humana agrupada exceden 500 participantes verificados (6 de 27 estudios). Los estudios en animales mostraron consistentemente citocinas proinflamatorias reducidas (TNF-α, IL-6) y activación de vías AMPK, pero la traducción a humanos espera ensayos más grandes y más prolongados.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: La calificación Moderada refleja evidencia humana sólida (11 ensayos) pero solo una revisión sistemática sin replicación independiente hasta la fecha. La precisión es modesta (~500 participantes verificados) y la heterogeneidad de resultados es mayor que la náusea — algunos ensayos miden dolor articular/función, otros biomarcadores séricos — haciendo que un único efecto agrupado sea menos interpretable. Los datos en animales son alentadores pero no elevan la calificación humana.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Solo un metanálisis en humanos (2019) sintetizó específicamente el efecto del jengibre en la pérdida de peso en sujetos con sobrepeso/obesos; los tamaños de muestra en esa síntesis no pudieron ser verificados a partir del resumen. Dos estudios en animales (2018, 2006) mostraron reducción del peso corporal y mejora de los marcadores metabólicos (glucosa, lípidos) a través de la regulación de microARN y AMPK en modelos de obesidad inducida por dieta y diabetes inducida por estreptozotocina.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: La calificación Emergente es apropiada porque la evidencia humana descansa en una única síntesis con precisión no confirmada, sin replicación independiente en ensayos humanos, y solo los datos en animales no pueden establecer eficacia clínica. Este resultado sigue siendo una hipótesis que espera ensayos humanos más grandes; el mecanismo es plausible pero la traducción a pérdida de peso sostenida en personas no está probada.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Siete estudios en humanos y seis estudios en animales examinaron resultados digestivos incluyendo gastroenteritis, gastroparesia inducida por quimioterapia, y motilidad gástrica postoperatoria. Un RCT de 2021 en niños con gastroenteritis aguda (n=150) encontró que el jengibre era efectivo como antiemérico. Múltiples ensayos combinaron jengibre con técnicas similares a acupresión. Los participantes humanos agrupados exceden 2.900 en cinco estudios con tamaños de muestra capturados. Los estudios en animales mostraron normalización de contracciones estomacales y marcadores inflamatorios reducidos en el tracto GI.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: La calificación Moderada refleja 7 RCT sólidos en humanos y una revisión sistemática, pero sin replicación independiente de esa síntesis hasta la fecha, y heterogeneidad moderada en definiciones de resultados (náusea vs. vómito vs. tiempo de vaciamiento gástrico vs. calambres). La precisión es buena (~2.900 participantes verificados) pero la consistencia en metanálisis independientes no está confirmada, manteniendo la calificación en Moderada en lugar de Fuerte.

explanation_es.evidence_base: El jengibre está respaldado por 19 estudios en humanos (principalmente ensayos controlados aleatorizados y revisiones sistemáticas, 2004–2026) y 25 estudios en animales. La evidencia en humanos es más sólida y más reciente para náusea/vómito (cuatro metanálisis independientes convergen), y sustancial para inflamación y función intestinal (aunque con solo metanálisis únicos cada uno). Los estudios en animales apoyan consistentemente los mecanismos pero no pueden establecer eficacia clínica por sí solos. El cuerpo de evidencia abarca dos décadas, con ensayos recientes de 2025–2026 añadiendo confianza a los resultados de inflamación e intestino.
explanation_es.open_questions: En los registros proporcionados, náusea/vómito es el resultado más replicado robustamente, mientras que inflamación y función intestinal descansan en metanálisis únicos (no verificados independientemente). La pérdida de peso es abordada por solo una síntesis en humanos y sigue siendo preliminar. Los ensayos recuperados inscriben principalmente adultos sometidos a cirugía, recibiendo quimioterapia, o con inflamación articular leve — la generalización al uso crónico en poblaciones sanas o a trastornos GI graves no se aborda en la muestra de registros mostrada. La mayoría de los ensayos se ejecutan durante 2–12 semanas; la seguridad y eficacia a largo plazo (más allá de 3–6 meses) no están capturadas en los resúmenes proporcionados.

appraisal_es.headline: La evidencia de náusea/vómito es fuerte y replicada en múltiples metanálisis; inflamación y digestión descansan en síntesis únicas sin replicación; la pérdida de peso es demasiado escasa para respaldar cualquier conclusión.

concerns.detail: El resultado de inflamación descansa en un solo metanálisis (2022, n=166), sin replicación independiente o síntesis que verifique su conclusión. El motor explícitamente señala 'existe un solo metanálisis / revisión sistemática, pero su conclusión no está replicada o verificada independientemente.' De 27 estudios totales, 16 son modelos animales—poco predictivos de la respuesta antiinflamatoria humana—dejando solo 11 estudios humanos para respaldar la calificación Moderada. Sin metanálisis humanos independientes que converjan en este hallazgo, la base de evidencia es frágil.

concerns.issue: Digestión: metanálisis único sin replicación, solapamiento importante con náusea postoperatoria
concerns.detail: Como la inflamación, la digestión/gut descansa en un metanálisis sin replicación (2023, n=2199). Críticamente, cinco de los siete estudios humanos listados (2023, 2024, 2024, 2022, 2004, 2020) abordan náusea y vómito postoperatorio—la misma población que el resultado 'náusea/vómito'. Esto significa que el resultado de digestión no es evidencia verdaderamente independiente; es en gran medida un recuento de los estudios de náusea bajo una etiqueta de resultado diferente. El verdadero cuerpo de evidencia de digestión independiente es mucho más pequeño de lo que los números sugieren.

concerns.issue: Pérdida de peso/grasa: base de evidencia mínima y no verificable
concerns.detail: Solo 3 estudios totales (1 metanálisis humano, 2 animales), sin tamaños de muestra extraíbles de los resúmenes. El motor señala 'los tamaños de muestra no pudieron ser verificados' y 'solo un estudio humano aborda este resultado; la consistencia no puede ser evaluada.' Un solo metanálisis humano no puede establecer consistencia o precisión. La calificación Emergente puede ser apropiada, pero este resultado tiene casi ningún peso evidencial y no debe impulsar decisiones clínicas.

concerns.issue: Náusea/vómito: la mayoría de resúmenes omiten tamaño de muestra; la precisión puede estar sobrestimada
concerns.detail: Aunque 9 de 20 estudios reportan n (mediana 150, ~3447 total), el motor señala 'la mayoría de resúmenes omiten tamaño de muestra, así que el total verdadero es sustancialmente mayor.' Esto significa que el tamaño de muestra verificado es incompleto y la precisión verdadera del efecto agrupado no puede confirmarse solo desde estos registros. Si los estudios no reportados son predominantemente pequeños, la razón de probabilidades agrupada (0.39 [0.16–0.96]) podría ser impulsada por pocos ensayos grandes; si son grandes, la precisión está subestimada. Los registros no permiten evaluar qué escenario se sostiene.

concerns.issue: Náusea/vómito: contextos clínicos heterogéneos, generalización poco clara
concerns.detail: Los 15 ECA abarcan náusea postoperatoria, náusea inducida por quimioterapia, náusea en embarazo, y gastroenteritis aguda en niños. Estos son escenarios fisiopatológicos distintos (postop ≠ quimioterapia ≠ embarazo). Los metanálisis no reportan heterogeneidad de subgrupo en estos registros, así que es poco claro si la jengibre es igualmente efectiva en todos los contextos o si su efecto es impulsado por un contexto. Agrupar etiologías dispares puede oscurecer la eficacia dependiente del contexto.

appraisal_es.mechanism_check: La jengibre contiene gingeroles y shogaoles, conocidos *in vitro* para modular receptores 5-HT3 y NK1 implicados en náusea. Este mecanismo es plausible para emesis postoperatoria e inducida por quimioterapia. Sin embargo, los estudios de inflamación miden marcadores (estrés oxidativo, citocinas) sin vincular directamente el mecanismo putativo de la jengibre (agonismo de receptores de gingerol) a resultados antiinflamatorios clínicos en humanos. El salto de mecanismo *in vitro* a reducción clínica de inflamación está presente pero no está fundamentado empíricamente en estos registros. Para digestión, ningún mecanismo está articulado en los resúmenes.
appraisal_es.strongest_counterargument: Un escéptico señalaría que la evidencia de náusea/vómito, aunque consistente, está dominada por un solo metanálisis de alta calidad de 2023 (n=2199) y tres metanálisis anteriores que probablemente extrajeron de conjuntos de ensayos superpuestos. Si esas cuatro síntesis están reanalizar los mismos ECA centrales, la aparente 'replicación' es un artefacto estadístico, no validación independiente. Además, la OR agrupada (0.39, IC 95% [0.16–0.96]) incluye 1.0 en el límite inferior del intervalo de confianza bajo algunas especificaciones de modelo, sugiriendo precisión marginal. Inflamación y digestión descansan en síntesis únicas sin replicación—muy por debajo del umbral 'fuerte'. La pérdida de peso es demasiado escasa para merecer inclusión.
appraisal_es.what_would_change_the_picture: Para inflamación y digestión: al menos dos metanálisis independientes o revisiones sistemáticas con poblaciones de ECA pre-especificadas y no superpuestas, o un ECA grande (n≥500), doble ciego en un contexto clínico único (p. ej., osteoartritis o EII) publicado después de 2022. Para náusea/vómito: metarregresión estratificada por contexto clínico (postop, quimioterapia, embarazo) para establecer si la eficacia es dependiente del contexto o universal, y replicación del efecto agrupado en un metanálisis prospectivo de datos de participantes individuales (IPD) para confirmar que la precisión no es impulsada por un ensayo atípico único.
